8. अन्य समितियां/बोर्ड 
8.4 लेखापरीक्षा समिति 


संस्थान की लेखापरीक्षा समिति की स्थापना परिषद्‌ द्वारा अप्रैल 2004 में एक स्पष्ट रूप से परिभाषित अधिदेश के साथ एक गैर- 
स्थायी समिति के रूप में की गई थी | अधिक स्वतंत्रता सुनिश्चित करने हेतु, वर्ष 2009 से इसकी अध्यक्षता अनन्य रूप से एक 
सरकारी नामनिर्देशिती द्वारा की जाती है । इसकी स्वायत्तता में और अधिक अभिवृद्धि हेतु, कार्यपालक समिति और वित्त समिति 
के सदस्यों को केंद्रीय लेखापरीक्षा समिति में सेवा करने की अनुमति नहीं है । इसके अतिरिक्त, पांच क्षेत्रीय लेखापरीक्षा समितियां 
- दक्षिणी, पश्चिमी, मध्य, उत्तरी और पूर्वी - समिति के कार्य का समर्थन करती हैं, जिससे क्षेत्रीय प्रतिनिधित्व और प्रभावी निगरानी 
सुनिश्चित होती है। 


समिति वित्तीय रिपोर्टिंग प्रक्रिया की निगरानी करने तथा संस्थान के वित्तीय प्रकटनों की सहीता, सत्यनिष्ठा और पारदर्शिता 
सुनिश्चित करने के लिए उत्तरदायी है। यह लेखापरीक्षा रिपोर्टों का पुनर्विलोकन करती है, लेखापरीक्षकों के साथ प्रेक्षणों पर विचार- 
विमर्श करती है, सुधारात्मक कार्रवाइयों की सिफारिश करती है और आंतरिक नियंत्रण परिवेश के सुदृढ़ीकरण हेतु प्रयासरत रहती 
है। समिति सुशासन और लेखापरीक्षा व्यवहारों में सतत सुधार के प्रति प्रतिबद्ध बनी हुई है | 


सांविधिक लेखापरीक्षा 


सांविधिक लेखापरीक्षकों की नियुक्ति : चार्टर्ड अकाउंटेंट अधिनियम, 4949 की धारा 48(5) के अनुसार, आईसीएआई 
की शाखाओं , क्षेत्रीय परिषदों, विकेंद्रीकृत कार्यालयों, उत्कृष्टता केंद्र और प्रधान कार्यालय हेतु सांविधिक लेखापरीक्षकों 
की नियुक्ति भारत के नियंत्रक और महालेखापरीक्षक (सी एंड एजी) द्वारा सिफारिश की गई दो फर्मों के पैनल में से, 
वित्तीय वर्ष 2022-23 से प्रभावी रूप से, की जाती है । यह प्रणाली निरंतरता सुनिश्चित करती है और लेखापरीक्षा 
विलंबों से बचाती है । इन नियुक्तियों पर एक स्थिति रिपोर्ट सी एंड एजी के साथ नियमित रूप से साझा की जाती है। 
लेखापरीक्षा रिपोर्टिंग ढांचा : सांविधिक लेखापरीक्षकों का रिपोर्टिंग ढांचा चार्टर्ड अकाउंटेंट्स विनियम, 988 के 
विनियम 496 और 49 द्वारा शासित होता है। 

संयुक्त सांविधिक लेखापरीक्षक : आईसीएआई प्रधान कार्यालय के लेखाओं की लेखापरीक्षा दो संयुक्त सांविधिक 
लेखापरीक्षकों द्वारा की जाती है, जो विविध विशेषज्ञता लाते हैं तथा व्यापक पुनर्विलोकन और उत्तरदायित्व सुनिश्चित 
करते हैं | 


आंतरिक लेखापरीक्षा 


आंतरिक लेखापरीक्षा व्याप्ति : एक हजार से अधिक सदस्यों वाली शाखाओं , क्षेत्रीय परिषदों, विकेंद्रीकृत कार्यालयों, 
THEM केंद्र और प्रधान कार्यालय सहित सभी प्रमुख इकाइयों हेतु एक सुदृढ़ आंतरिक लेखापरीक्षा तंत्र विद्यमान है। 
आंतरिक लेखापरीक्षा लेखापरीक्षा समिति के पर्यवेक्षण के अधीन की जाती है, जो पारदर्शिता और लेखापरीक्षक स्वतंत्रता 
सुनिश्चित करती है। 

ईओआई के माध्यम से नियुक्ति : आंतरिक लेखापरीक्षकों की नियुक्ति सीए फर्मों से रुचि की अभिव्यक्ति (ईओआई) हेतु 
खुले आमंत्रण की एक पारदर्शी प्रक्रिया के माध्यम से की जाती है । चयन एक वस्तुनिष्ठ मूल्यांकन और रैंकिंग प्रणाली पर 
आधारित होता है। लेखापरीक्षाएं अर्धवार्षिक रूप से की जाती हैं और विहित कार्यक्षेत्र और रिपोर्टिंग प्रारूप के अनुसार 
वित्तीय और अनुपालन, दोनों पहलुओं को सम्मिलित करती हैं । लेखापरीक्षा रिपोर्टों का अनुवर्ती कार्रवाई हेतु संबंधित 
क्षेत्रीय या केंद्रीय लेखापरीक्षा समितियों द्वारा पुनर्विलोकन किया जाता है।

No. -CA(5)/77/2026.—In pursuance of sub-Section (5B) of Section 8 of the Chartered

Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) for the year ended 3i%t March 2026 is hereby published for

777 Annual Report 
Transforming Profession: Building Trust, Embracing Innovation, Strengthening Nation 
Building Trust 


The story of India’s rise as a leading global economy is not merely a story of economic expansion; it is 
a story of trust, innovation, and institutional strength. At every stage of this journey, the accountancy 
profession has served as a vital enabler, providing the credibility, transparency, and confidence 
necessary for sustainable progress. As the nation advances towards the vision of Viksit Bharat, the 
Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) continues to play a transformative role by nurturing 
a profession that combines integrity with innovation and expertise with public purpose. 


Trust remains the cornerstone of economic development. Investors, businesses, governments, and 
citizens rely on accurate and transparent financial information to make informed decisions. Chartered 
Accountants have long been the custodians of this trust, ensuring that financial reporting, and 
governance frameworks operate with the highest standards of professionalism and accountability. 
Through their commitment to ethics and public interest, they strengthen the foundations of markets, 
reinforce confidence in institutions, and contribute to a stable and resilient economic ecosystem. 


As economic activities become increasingly interconnected across borders, trust must extend beyond 
national boundaries. Indian businesses today operate in a global environment where comparability, 
consistency, and credibility of financial information are indispensable. ICAI has actively facilitated this 
transition by aligning professional standards with international best practices, promoting global 
partnerships, and strengthening the international mobility of Indian professionals. These efforts have 
enhanced the reputation of the Indian accountancy profession and positioned Chartered Accountants 
as trusted contributors to the global economy. 


Embracing Innovation 


The profession is simultaneously undergoing a profound transformation driven by technology. Artificial 
intelligence, machine learning, blockchain, data analytics, and automation are redefining how financial 
information is generated, analysed, and assured. Rather than viewing these developments as 
disruptions, ICAI has embraced them as opportunities to elevate professional value. By equipping 
members with future-oriented skills and encouraging the adoption of advanced technologies, the 
Institute is enabling a shift from traditional compliance-driven functions towards strategic advisory, 
predictive insights, and value creation. 


Innovation within the profession extends beyond technology. It encompasses new approaches to 
governance, risk management, sustainability, and stakeholder engagement. Modern enterprises are 
increasingly evaluated not only by financial performance but also by their environmental and social 
impact. Recognising this evolution, ICAI has been at the forefront of developing professional capabilities 
in sustainability reporting, ESG assurance, integrated reporting, and responsible business practices. By

5. DISCIPLINARY DIRECTORATE 


The Disciplinary Directorate, which serves as the regulatory arm of ICAI, has been established to 
examine cases of alleged professional or other misconduct by its members. Such cases may be initiated 
either through a formal complaint filed in Form I or through information received under the provisions 
of the Chartered Accountants Act, 949 and/or the Rules framed thereunder. 


Under this disciplinary framework, the Directorate is entrusted with the responsibility of investigating 
any alleged lapses or irregularities committed by members across the country. This ensures that public 
confidence in the profession is maintained, while also setting clear standards of acceptable professional 
conduct. Although the majority of members contribute responsibly and diligently to society through 
their expertise, the disciplinary mechanism exists to take corrective action against the few who deviate 
from the expected standards. 


Following the amendments to the Chartered Accountants Act, 949 in 2006, the disciplinary mechanism 
underwent significant reforms aimed at improving the efficiency and speed of disposal of disciplinary 
cases. Currently, the system operates through two quasi-judicial bodies established under the Chartered 
Accountants (Amendment) Act, 2006, namely the Board of Discipline under Section 2iA and the 
Disciplinary Committee under Section 2iB. The structure and processes of this mechanism are designed 
to ensure transparency, strengthen public trust and provide fair and impartial justice to members facing 
allegations of misconduct. To further enhance accountability among members and firms, and to ensure 
timely delivery of justice, the Act was amended again in 2022; however, the effective date for the 
implementation of the revised disciplinary provisions is yet to be notified. 


During the Council Year 2025-26, four Benches of the Disciplinary Committee, i.e. Bench I, Bench II, 
Bench III (including MNAF cases) and Bench IV, and one Bench of the Board of Discipline were 
constituted for the expeditious disposal of cases under enquiry, apart from the consideration of the 
Prima Facie Opinions formed by the Director (Discipline). In addition, the Disciplinary Committee under 
Section 2iD, headed by the President, ICAI, was also constituted to look into any residual old cases 
that are/may be referred back. 


The disciplinary mechanism of ICAI has evolved into a comprehensive and robust regulatory framework 
capable of addressing professional misconduct in an increasingly complex financial ecosystem. The 
transition from a Council-centric model to a multi-tiered, independent and structured system reflects a 
deliberate and progressive reform process. The evolving disciplinary architecture stands as a critical 
pillar in preserving the integrity, credibility, and accountability of the profession, ensuring that it remains 
aligned with both domestic expectations and global standards.

6.2 AUDITING AND ASSURANCE STANDARDS BOARD (AASB) 


Audit plays a critical role in protecting public interest by enhancing accountability and fostering trust in 
financial reporting, thereby supporting economic growth. Increasing business complexity and 
expanding global operations have enhanced stakeholder expectations of the auditing profession. The 
ICAI's Auditing and Assurance Standards Board (AASB) develops high-quality Standards on Auditing, 
Review, Assurance, Quality Control/Quality Management, and Related Services, which set best practices 
and serve as benchmarks for auditor performance. 


The Board also issues Guidance Notes on general and industry-specific auditing issues to provide 
practical support to auditors. These are released under the ICAI Council's authority, except for auditing 
standards relating to companies and Limited Liability Partnerships (LLPs), where the Central 
Government prescribes standards based on ICAI’s recommendations, in consultation with the National 
Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA). ICAI’s auditing standards are harmonised with those of the 
International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board (IAASB) to maintain global consistency. To aid 
effective implementation, the Board publishes Technical Guides, Practice Manuals, Studies and

Implementation Guides, offering members practical tools to navigate complex audit scenarios 
confidently. 


The following is a comprehensive overview of the important achievements of the Board: 
(I) Representations/Suggestions to Ministries and Regulators 
ICAI’s Recommendations on Standards on Auditing for Audit of LLPs 


In August 2024, the Board submitted ICAI’s recommendations on the Standards on Auditing for audit 
of LLPs (“SAs for LLPs”) to NFRA for notification under Section 34A of the LLP Act, 2008, recommending 
that the SAs recommended by ICAI to NFRA for audit of companies should apply mutatis mutandis to 
the audit of LLPs. Subsequently, the MCA directed ICAI to develop a separate set of SAs for LLPs. In 
response, the Board developed a separate set of SAs for LLPs, which was considered and approved by 
the Council of ICAI. ICAI's final recommendations on SAs for LLPs were submitted to NFRA vide letter 
dated 247 June, 2025. 


Development of Digital Balance Confirmation Portal (DBCP) 


ICAI has entered into a tri-party MoU with the Indian Banks’ Association (IBA) and PSB Alliance Private 
Limited to develop the Digital Balance Confirmation Portal (DBCP), a platform enabling auditors to 
obtain digitally signed balance confirmations directly from banks. The portal underwent multiple 
demonstrations in 2024, followed by testing sessions in January 2025. Phase I (Beta) was launched 
with Canara Bank on 2™ February 2025 during the World Forum of Accountants, and further testing 
took place in June 2025 with ICAI, PSB Alliance and NeSL. The portal is currently live with 9 banks, viz. 
Canara Bank, UCO Bank, Punjab National Bank, Bank of Maharashtra, Indian Overseas Bank, Punjab & 
Sind Bank, Bank of Baroda, Bank of India and Union Bank of India. A user guidance manual has been 
developed, and the platform will gradually be extended to more banks, co-operative banks and financial 
institutions. Overall, the DBCP represents a major step towards digital transformation in audit 
confirmations, improving transparency, efficiency and reliability. 


Capacity Building Programme for Officers of the C&AG 


ICAI, in collaboration with the Office of the Comptroller & Auditor General (C&AG) of India, organised 
a Capacity Building Programme for officers of the C&AG engaged in the audit of PSUs at ICAI’s Centre 
of Excellence, Hyderabad. Phase I was conducted from 57 May, 2025 to 47 June 2025, Phase II from 
27" October, 2025 to i8 November, 2025 and Phase III from 97 March, 2026 to 77 April, 2026, all at 
the same venue. The programme covered a wide range of topics, including Indian Accounting Standards 
(Ind AS), Standards on Auditing (SAs), sector-specific audit areas and information technology-related 
aspects. The AASB supported the auditing-related sessions by developing background material and 
arranging faculty with the requisite subject-matter expertise.

Retirement Funds of Companies under C&AG Audit 


At the request of the Office of the C&AG, the Board developed a Checklist for Safeguards and Risk 
Management in respect of Trusts managing post-retirement funds of companies under C&AG audit. The 
checklist was submitted to the Office of the C&AG vide email dated 3' February, 2026.

Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 952, and to develop the audit report format for 
such PF Trusts. The Board developed the audit report format for PF Trusts and submitted it to the 
EPFO.

6.4 INTERNAL AUDIT STANDARDS BOARD (IASB) 


The Internal Audit Standards Board (IASB) of ICAI plays a crucial role in regulating and enhancing the

comprehensive framework for internal auditors to perform their duties effectively, ensuring consistency, 
objectivity and professionalism in their engagements. By setting benchmarks for internal audit 
processes, reporting and ethical conduct, the Board contributes significantly to strengthening corporate 
governance, risk management and internal control systems within organisations across various sectors. 
The key activities of the Board during the period under report are as under: 


(I) Certificate Course on Concurrent Audit of Banks 


The Board conducts the Certificate Course on Concurrent Audit of Banks to enable members to 
supplement the efforts of banks in carrying out internal checks of transactions and other verifications 
and compliance with the procedures laid down, improve the effectiveness of the concurrent audit 
system in banks, improve the quality and coverage of concurrent audit reports and understand the 
intricacies of concurrent audit of banks. During the period, the Board organised 28 batches of the 
Course in physical mode, and around ,606 participants successfully completed the Course.

The Certificate Course on Internal Audit has been completely revamped by the Board with new topics 
and a strong information technology component, and launched in a contemporary format to serve the 
needs of all stakeholders. The Course has been designed to enhance the expertise of Chartered 
Accountants in Internal Audit, build Governance, Risk and Compliance as one of their core competencies 
and help certified members distinguish themselves from others conducting internal audits. During the 
period, the Board organised i batch of the Course in physical mode, and around 243 participants 
successfully completed the Course.

6.8 PEER REVIEW BOARD 


The Peer Review mechanism was introduced by the Council of ICAI with the setting up of the Peer 
Review Board in March 2002. The Board has since been progressing satisfactorily and continuously 
providing guidance to members to enhance the efficiency of assurance services rendered by them. The 
main objective of Peer Review is to ensure that in carrying out an assurance service assignment, the 
member (a) complies with Technical, Professional and Ethical Standards as applicable, including other 
regulatory requirements; and (b) has in place proper systems, including documentation thereof, to 
amply demonstrate the quality of the assurance services. The Peer Review is conducted of a Practice 
Unit by an independent evaluator known as a Reviewer.

Firms/LLPs and appointment of auditors of companies under Sections i39(5) and i39(7) of the

6.4 EXPERT ADVISORY COMMITTEE (EAC) 


In a dynamic economic landscape marked by increasingly complex transactions and the continuous 
evolution of financial reporting requirements, accounting professionals are often required to address 
intricate and emerging issues. Such situations demand professional judgement supported by well- 
reasoned and authoritative guidance to maintain the credibility and quality of financial reporting. The 
Expert Advisory Committee (EAC) serves as a key technical body in this regard by providing independent 
and well-deliberated opinions on intricate accounting matters. Over the years, the Committee has 
established itself as a valuable and trusted source of technical guidance, assisting members across 
industries, as well as government and regulatory institutions, in addressing practical accounting 
challenges. 


(I) Expert Opinions 


The Committee responds to queries from members strictly in line with the Advisory Service Rules. Its 
scope is confined to issues relating to accounting and auditing principles; accordingly, issues involving 
the legal interpretation of statutory enactments and/or cases of professional misconduct are not 
answered by it. Further, as per the Rules, matters pending before the Board of Discipline or the 
Disciplinary Committee of the Institute, or before an appropriate department of the Government or the 
Income-tax authorities, are not answered by the Committee. The Advisory Service Rules are accessible 


on the ICAI website(https://www.icai.org/post/495) 


The opinions issued by the Expert Advisory Committee are based on the specific facts and circumstances 
provided by the querist, taking into account the relevant laws, statutes and applicable accounting and 
auditing principles. Each opinion clearly states the date of its finalisation and should be read considering 
the developments and/or amendments to laws or standards that may have occurred after that date. 


(II) Opinions Finalised 


During the period from * April, 2025 to 30 April, 2026, the Committee finalised forty-three (43) 
opinions on a wide range of queries raised by members involving issues related to accounting principles.

8.4 AUDIT COMMITTEE 


The Audit Committee of the Institute was established in April 200i by the Council as a non-standing 
committee with a clearly defined mandate. Since 2009, it has been chaired exclusively by a Government 
Nominee to ensure greater independence. To further enhance its autonomy, members of the Executive 
Committee and the Finance Committee are not permitted to serve on the Central Audit Committee. 
Additionally, five Regional Audit Committees — Southern, Western, Central, Northern and Eastern — 
support the Committee’s work, ensuring regional representation and effective oversight. 


The Committee is responsible for overseeing the financial reporting process and ensuring the accuracy, 
integrity and transparency of the Institute’s financial disclosures. It reviews audit reports, discusses 
observations with the auditors, recommends corrective actions and strives to strengthen the internal 
control environment. The Committee remains committed to good governance and continuous 
improvement in audit practices. 


Statutory Audit 


e Appointment of Statutory Auditors: In accordance with Section i8(5) of the Chartered 
Accountants Act, i949, the statutory auditors for ICAI’s Branches, Regional Councils, 
Decentralised Offices, Centre of Excellence and Head Office are appointed from a panel of two 
firms recommended by the Comptroller and Auditor General (C&AG) of India, effective from FY 
2022-23. This system ensures continuity and avoids audit delays. A status report on these 
appointments is regularly shared with the C&AG. 

e Audit Reporting Framework: The statutory auditors’ reporting framework is governed by 
Regulations 96 and 97 of the Chartered Accountants Regulations, 988. 

¢ Joint Statutory Auditors: The accounts of the ICAI Head Office are audited by two joint 
statutory auditors, bringing diverse expertise and ensuring comprehensive review and 
accountability. 


Internal Audit 


e Internal Audit Coverage: A robust internal audit mechanism is in place for all major units, 
including branches with over a thousand members, Regional Councils, Decentralised Offices, the 
Centre of Excellence and the Head Office. The internal audit is conducted under the supervision 
of the Audit Committee, which ensures transparency and auditor independence. 


e Appointment through 50: Internal auditors are appointed through a transparent process 
involving an open invitation for Expressions of Interest (50) from CA firms. Selection is based 
on an objective evaluation and ranking system. Audits are conducted biannually and cover both 
financial and compliance aspects, as per the prescribed scope and reporting format. Audit reports 
are reviewed by the respective Regional or Central Audit Committees for follow-up action.

9.7 GRIEVANCE RESOLUTION DIRECTORATE 


Grievance Resolution Directorate (GRD) (now merged with Members & Students Services Directorate) 
was a centralized department of ICAI formed to oversee the support system for our students, members 
and other stakeholders for their engagement with institute's various activities which is delivered through 
multiple departments, committees dealing in respective areas. The GRD facilitates timely and effective 
grievance redressal through multiple channels, including Call Sahayata, E-Sahayata, dedicated email 
support, and social media. The Directorate focuses on active process monitoring, timeliness, root cause 
analysis, coordination with all stakeholders ensuring transparency, trust, and overall stakeholder 
satisfaction. 


Call Sahayata 


ICAI Call Sahayata (9997599975) operates from 09:00 AM To 09:00 PM, Monday to Saturday, except 
on gazetted holidays, enabling students, members and stakeholders to reach ICAI primarily through 
inbound calls for their queries. Calls received during operational hours are routed through and 
Interactive Voice Response(IVR) system, ensuring effective inbound calls management. Queries 
received outside operational hours are captured through the IVR and are addressed during working 
hours through callbacks. The helpline handles both general information and service-related queries in 
an efficient and systematic manner.

to protect and defend the interest of the Institute in the cases filed against it, provides legal opinions 
to various Departments within ICAI on adherence to the statutory mandate, defends regulatory actions

in various courts, collaborates with other Departments to enforce regulations and penalize violations as 
per the statutory mandate. 


The significant legal developments concerning the Institute and the profession during the year are as 
under: 


(I) Supreme Court Rules in Favour of Chartered Accountants — Parity with Advocates for 
Appointment as Member (Accountant), ITAT 


The Hon’ble Supreme Court restored parity between Chartered Accountants and Advocates in the 
matter of the minimum experience criteria for appointment as Members of the Income Tax Appellate 
Tribunal (ITAT). In a landmark judgement pronounced on 20th November 2025, a Bench of the Hon’ble 
Supreme Court comprising the Chief Justice of India and Justice K. Vinod Chandran invalidated the rule 
requiring 25 years of experience for the post of Member (Accountant) of the ITAT. The ruling places 
Chartered Accountants on a par with Advocates regarding the minimum experience criteria and sets 
right the injustice to Chartered Accountants under the Rules, which prescribed a minimum experience 
of 25 years for a Chartered Accountant to be considered for the post of Member (Accountant) as against 
only i0 years for Advocates to be considered for the post of Member (Judicial). 


Historically, the minimum experience requirements for both Chartered Accountants and Advocates were 
the same, before the new Rules disturbed this parity to the disadvantage of Chartered Accountants. 


The judgement restores the status quo between Advocates and Chartered Accountants in the matter 
of the minimum experience requirement, which had occupied the field for many years. 


(II) Directions of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Himanshu Singh vs. UOI (the “Supertech 
Case”) 


The Hon’ble Supreme Court of India, on 29th April 2025, in the case of Himanshu Singh vs. Union of 
India (popularly known as the Supertech Case), issued various directions to the Government of India, 
the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, RERA, the RBI, the CBI and ICAI. More than 70 petitions 
were filed by over ,200 home buyers in the Supreme Court alleging the systematic failure of statutory 
and government authorities to discharge their statutory functions, the circumvention of the regulatory 
framework by banks and housing finance corporations, and the resultant illicit benefits said to have 
been drawn by builders/developers, with home buyers bearing the brunt of such failures. 


In so far as ICAI is concerned, the Hon’ble Court directed as follows: 


79, The President, Institute of Chartered Accountants of India is directed to deploy three Chartered 
Accountants, who are well conversant with the process of forensic audit and place them at the disposal 
of CBI to assist the Bureau/SIT in the matter of subject enquiry/investigations. The details of the 
remuneration to be paid to these Chartered Accountants be forwarded to this Court so that an 
appropriate order in that regard can be passed on the next date of hearing.”

9.l PUBLICATION DIRECTORATE 


The Publication Directorate (erstwhile Publication & CDS Directorate) plays a pivotal role in ensuring 
the availability of ICAI’s educational and professional publications to students, members, and other 
stakeholders. The Directorate oversees the printing, inventory management, distribution, and 
accounting of study materials, member publications, and other official publications of the Institute. The 
Directorate manages the Institute’s online Publication Portal (https://cds.icai.org/), which enables 
stakeholders to purchase publications and artefacts through a seamless digital platform. The portal 
supports online ordering, payment processing, and delivery through the Centralized Distribution System 
(CDS), thereby enhancing accessibility and service efficiency. 


To maintain an efficient supply chain, the Directorate administers inventory across designated storage 
locations and undertakes periodic physical stock verification. Stock valuation and inventory records are 
maintained in coordination with the Accounts Department to support accurate financial reporting and 
effective inventory control. The Directorate also undertakes reconciliation of publication sales with 
payment gateway collections and facilitates the integration of sales and dispatch information with the 
Institute’s ERP system. This ensures transparency, accuracy, and timely accounting of publication- 
related transactions. Through these functions, the Publication Directorate contributes significantly to 
the Institute’s objective of providing timely access to quality educational resources while maintaining 
robust inventory management, financial discipline, and operational transparency.

9.5 UDIN DIRECTORATE 


The Unique Document Identification Number (UDIN), introduced by ICAI, continues to play a pivotal 
role in ensuring the authenticity, reliability and transparency of documents certified by Chartered 
Accountants. By assigning a system-generated unique identification number to every certificate, audit 
report and attestation, UDIN serves as a robust mechanism to prevent document forgery and misuse. 
Over the years, UDIN has evolved into a critical component of the regulatory ecosystem, facilitating 
seamless verification of documents by regulators, government authorities, financial institutions and 
other users. During the year under review, UDIN witnessed significant advancements in technological 
transformation, regulatory integration and functional enhancements.

The ICAI Placement Directorate of The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India was formed in the 
year 2026 with the objective of creating a dedicated and focused platform for facilitating career 
opportunities for Chartered Accountants and strengthening industry-profession engagement. The 
Directorate acts as a bridge between industry and the Chartered Accountancy profession by providing 
structured, transparent, and technology-driven placement and career support services for Newly 
Qualified Chartered Accountants (NQCAs), Experienced Chartered Accountants, semi-qualified 
professionals, and organizations across diverse sectors and geographies. 


With a vision to empower finance professionals and support organizations in accessing quality talent, 
the ICAI Placement Directorate undertakes various initiatives including Campus Placement 
Programmes, ICAI Campus Placement+, Career Ascent Programmes, HR Meets, Overseas Placement 
Initiatives, CA Career Catalyst Programmes, Orientation Programmes, and Management Development 
Programmes (MDPs) for CA Rank Holders. The Directorate also offers continuous recruitment and 
networking support through its digital platforms, enabling organizations to connect with highly skilled 
finance professionals throughout the year while helping Chartered Accountants explore opportunities 
across domains 


The major initiatives are as under: 
(I) CA Career Catalyst Programme 2026 


The Directorate launched the CA Career Catalyst Programme 2026, a comprehensive virtual career- 
readiness initiative designed for newly qualified Chartered Accountants and CA Final qualified 
candidates, conducted from i5th to 22nd March 2026 in a phased manner. During the period from i5th 
to 20th March 2026, domain-focused webinar sessions were organised daily covering important sectors 
and emerging career opportunities for Chartered Accountants, including taxation, mergers and 
acquisitions, finance, investment banking, statutory audit, internal audit, financial due diligence, 
forensic accounting, consultancy, advisory, FP&A, costing, budgeting and offshore opportunities. 


Further, on 2ist and 22nd March 2026, structured sessions on Group Discussion, HR Training, Mock 
Interviews and One-to-One Mentoring were organised in batches to equip participants with placement 
readiness, sector-selection guidance and interview preparedness. The programme received an 
encouraging response and served as a structured bridge between the declaration of the CA Final results 
and the commencement of placement activities.

i2 QUALITY REVIEW BOARD (QRB) 


The Quality Review Board (QRB), established by the Central Government of India under Section 28A of 
the Chartered Accountants Act, 949 (The ‘Act’), operates as an independent body to review the quality 
of services rendered by Chartered Accountants in India. The constitution of the Board consists of a 
Chairperson, five members appointed by the Central Government, and five members nominated by the 
Council of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI), ensuring a balanced governance 
structure. 


While statutorily empowered to examine quality of all professional services under Sec. 28B of the Act, 
the QRB is presently engaged in the review of quality of statutory audit services. In accordance with 
Section 28B, its principal functions consist of: 


e To make recommendations to the Council with regard to the quality of services provided by the 
members of the Institute. 

e To review the quality of services provided by the members of the Institute including audit 
services. 

e To guide the members of the Institute to improve the quality of services and adherence to the 
various statutory and other regulatory requirements. 

e To forward cases of non-compliance with various statutory and regulatory requirements by the 
members of the Institute or firms, noticed by it during the course of its reviews, to the 
Disciplinary Directorate for its examination. 


Subsequent to the establishment of National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) by the Central 
Government in 20i8, the jurisdiction of QRB has been correspondingly defined. The QRB is now 
mandated to undertake reviews of audit quality in respect of entities falling outside the ambit of Rule 
3 of the NFRA Rules, 208, as well as those referred to QRB by NFRA under Rule 9(4) of NFRA Rules, 
208.

INDEPENDENT AUDITOR’S REPORT 
To the Council of The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India 
Report on the Audit of the Financial Statements 
Opinion 


We have audited the accompanying financial statements of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India 
(‘the Institute”), which comprise the Balance Sheet as at March 3i, 2026, the Statement of Income and 
Expenditure, the Statement of Cash Flows for the year then ended, and notes to the financial statements, 
including a summary of significant accounting policies and other explanatory information (hereinafter 
referred to as “financial statements”) in which are incorporated the returns/financial statements audited by 
the branch auditors of Institute’s Decentralized offices, Overseas offices, Centers of Excellence, Regional 
Councils and their Branches. 


In our opinion and to the best of our information and according to the explanations given to us, the 
aforesaid financial statements give the information required by the Chartered Accountants Act, 949 (as 
amended up to date) and give a true and fair view in conformity with the accounting principles generally 
accepted in India, of the state of affairs of the Institute as at March 3i, 2026, and its surplus and its cash 
flows for the year ended on that date. 


Basis for Opinion 


We conducted our audit in accordance with the Standards on Auditing (SAs) issued by the Institute of 
Chartered Accountants of India. Our responsibilities under those Standards are further described in the 
‘Auditor’s Responsibilities for the Audit of the Financial Statements’ section of our report. We are 
independent of the Institute in accordance with the Code of Ethics issued by the Institute of Chartered 
Accountants of India (ICAI) together with the ethical requirements that are relevant to our audit of the 
financial statements and we have fulfilled our other ethical responsibilities in accordance with these 
requirements. We believe that the audit evidence we have obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide 
a basis for our opinion on the financial statements. 


Responsibilities of Management and those charged with governance for the Financial 
Statements 


The Institute’s Management and those charged with governance are responsible for the preparation of 
these financial statements that give a true and fair view of the financial position, financial performance, 
and cash flows of the Institute in accordance with the Chartered Accountants Act, 949 (“the Act”) This 
responsibility also includes maintenance of adequate accounting records in accordance with the provisions 
of the Act for safeguarding the assets of the Institute and for preventing and detecting frauds and other 
irregularities; selection and application of appropriate accounting policies; making judgments and estimates 
that are reasonable and prudent; and design, implementation and maintenance of adequate internal 
financial controls, that were operating effectively for ensuring the accuracy and completeness of the 
accounting records, relevant to the preparation and presentation of the financial statements that give a 
true and fair view and are free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error.

In preparing the financial statements, the management and those charged with governance are responsible 
for assessing the Institute’s ability to continue as a going concern, disclosing, as applicable, matters related 
to going concern and using the going concern basis of accounting unless the management and those 
charged with governance either intends to liquidate the Institute or to cease operations, or has no realistic 
alternative but to do so. 


Those charged with governance are also responsible for overseeing the Institute’s financial reporting 
process. 


Auditor’s Responsibilities for the Audit of the Financial Statements 


Our objectives are to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the financial statements as a whole are 
free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error, and to issue an auditor’s report that 
includes our opinion. Reasonable assurance is a high level of assurance, but is not a guarantee that an 
audit conducted in accordance with SAs will always detect a material misstatement when it exists. 
Misstatements can arise from fraud or error and are considered material if, individually or in the aggregate, 
they could reasonably be expected to influence the economic decisions of users taken on the basis of these 
financial statements. 


As part of an audit in accordance with SAs, we exercise professional judgment and maintain professional 
skepticism throughout the audit. We also: 


¢ Identify and assess the risks of material misstatement of the financial statements, whether due to fraud 
or error, design and perform audit procedures responsive to those risks, and obtain audit evidence that 
is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for our opinion. The risk of not detecting a material 
misstatement resulting from fraud is higher than for one resulting from error, as fraud may involve 
collusion, forgery, intentional omissions, misrepresentations, or the override of internal controls. 


¢ Obtain an understanding of internal controls relevant to the audit in order to design audit procedures 
that are appropriate in the circumstances, but not for the purpose of expressing an opinion on the 
effectiveness of the Institute’s internal controls. 


¢ Evaluate the appropriateness of accounting policies used and the reasonableness of accounting 
estimates and related disclosures made by management. 


¢ Conclude on the appropriateness of the management and those charged with governance’s use of the 
going concern basis of accounting and, based on the audit evidence obtained, whether a material 
uncertainty exists related to events or conditions that may cast significant doubt on the Institute’s 
ability to continue as a going concern. If we conclude that a material uncertainty exists, we are required 
to draw attention in our auditor’s report to the related disclosures in the financial statements or, if such 
disclosures are inadequate, to modify our opinion. Our conclusions are based on the audit evidence 
obtained up to the date of our auditor’s report. However, future events or conditions may cause the 
Institute to cease to continue as a going concern. 


¢ Evaluate the overall presentation, structure and content of the financial statements, including the 
disclosures, and whether the financial statements represent the underlying transactions and events in 
a manner that achieves fair presentation. 


-  Materiality is the magnitude of misstatements in the financial statements that, individually or in 
aggregate, makes it probable that the economic decisions of a reasonably knowledgeable user of the 
financial statements may be influenced. We consider quantitative materiality and qualitative factors in 
(i) planning the scope of our audit work and in evaluating the results of our work; and (ii) to evaluate 
the effect of any identified misstatements in the financial statements.

General Information 


The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India ("the Institute or ICAI"), having its Head Office 
at New Delhi, was established on ist July 949 by an Act of Parliament viz. The Chartered 
Accountants Act, 949 for the purpose of regulation and development of the profession of 
Chartered Accountants in India. In terms of the said Act, the Council of the Institute is 
entrusted with the task of managing the affairs of the Institute. For this purpose, the Council 
has constituted 5 Regional Councils, one each at Mumbai, Kolkata, Kanpur, Chennai and New 
Delhi, 5 Decentralised Offices, 3 Centres of Excellence, 86 branches and 2 overseas offices 
in Dubai & Singapore. 


Significant Accounting Policies 
Basis of Preparation 


The financial statements comprising Balance Sheet, Statement of Income and Expenditure , 
Statement of Cash Flows and Notes to Accounts thereon are prepared in accordance with the 
Generally Accepted Accounting Principles in India (Indian GAAP) and The Chartered 
Accountants Act,l949. Indian GAAP here comprises of the accounting standards and other 
pronouncements issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India.The financial 
statements are prepared on historical cost convention,going concern and on accrual basis unless 
other wise stated. The accounting polices adopted in the preparation of the financial statements 
are consistent with those followed in the previous year,unless stated otherwise. 


The Financial Statements are prepared in Indian Rupees (2) which is the functional and 
reporting currency of the Institute. All amounts disclosed in the financial Statement are rounded 
off to the nearest lakhs unless otherwise stated. 


Use of Estimates 

The preparation of the financial statements in conformity with Indian GAAP requires the 
Management to make estimates and assumptions considered in the reported amounts of assets 
and liabilities (including contingent liabilities) and the reported income and expenses of the 
year. The Management believes that the estimates used in preparation of the financial 
statements are prudent and reasonable. Actual results could differ from the estimates and the 
differences between the actual results and the estimates are recognised in the periods in 
which the results are known / materialised. 


Inventories 

Inventories comprise publications, study materials, stationery and other stores. Inventories are 
valued at the lower of cost based on first in first out method ("FIFO") and the net realisable 
value after providing for obsolescence and other losses, where considered necessary. 


Cost includes all charges in bringing the goods to the point of sale, including other levies, transit 
insurance and incidental charges. 


Cash and cash equivalents 

Cash comprises cash on hand. Cash equivalents are balances with banks and short-term 
balances (with an original maturity of three months or less from the date of acquisition), highly 
liquid investments that are readily convertible into known amounts of cash and which are 
subject to insignificant risk of changes in value. Fixed Deposits with original maturity of less 
than three months are considered as cash and cash equivalents. Deposits with original

under "Other bank balances". 


2.05 Statement of Cash Flows 
Cash flows are reported using the indirect method, whereby net surplus is adjusted for the 
effects of transactions of non-cash nature and any deferrals or accruals of past or future cash 
receipts or payments. The cash flows from operating, investing and financing activities of the 
Institute are segregated based on the basis of their nature. 


2.06 Appropriation to Reserves/ Funds 


i) Donations received for buildings are appropriated to income and expenditure account 
and then credited to the Infrastructure Reserve account. 


ii) 25% of the Distance Education Fee, not exceeding 50% of the net surplus of the 
year is transferred to Education Fund. 


iii) 0.75% of Membership Fee (Annual and Certificate of Practice Fee) due on accrual basis 
is transferred to the Employees’ Benevolent Fund. 


iv) Entrance & Admission Fee: 
- 2/3rd portion of the entrance fee from Associate members and Admission Fee from Fellow 
Members is taken to Infrastructure Reserve Account ; 


v) From the designated funds, the following transfers are made to Education Reserve Account: 


a) From Accounting ResearchBuilding 00% of cost of additions (net of deductions if 
Fund any) to Building Fund relating to Accounting 
Research Building Fund. 


b) From Education Fund 50% of cost of additions (net of deductions if any) 
to Fixed Assets. 


However, the appropriations to the aforesaid various reserves/funds is done on pro-rata basis by 
restricting the same to the amount of available surplus. 


vi) Income from investments is allocated based on opening balances of the respective 
Designated Funds and Restricted Funds on weighted average basis. 


vii) 25% of the Information Technology Training (ITT)/Advance Information Technology 
Training course Fee received during the year is transferred to ITT Reserve for replacement 
of computers and other ITT centre infrastructure. 


viii) A sum equal to depreciation for the year (excluding amount transferred to the ITT 
Reserve) is transferred to Sinking Fund for repair and replacement of assets. 


ix) The contribution to the restricted funds is directly taken to the Funds treating it as Corpus.

measured reliably. Property, Plant and Equipment are carried at cost less accumulated

Intangible Assets 

Intangible assets are carried at cost less accumulated amortisation and accumulated impairment

discounts and rebates, import duties and other taxes (other than those subsequently 
recoverable from the tax authorities), directly attributable expenditure on making the asset

to acquisition of qualifying assets up to the date the asset is ready for its intended use. 
Subsequent expenditure on intangible assets after its purchase / completion is capitalised 
only if such expenditure results in an increase in the future benefits from such asset beyond 
its previously assessed standard of performance. 


Capital Work in Progress 

Expenditure incurred on construction/ development of assets which is not ready for their 
intended use is carried at cost less impairment,if any, under Capital Work-in-Progress. The 
cost includes the purchase cost including import duties, non-refundable taxes, if any, and 
directly attributable costs.

Investment 

a) The Institute’s investments comprise of instruments in the form of domestic government 
securities issued by Central and State Governments, fixed deposits with scheduled banks 
domiciled in India and equity shares in Not-for-Profit entities. 


b) Investments are classified as current and non-current investments in accordance with AS 
i3 "Accounting for Investments". Current investments are those that are readily 
realisable and intended to be held for not more than one year from the date on which 
such investments are made. A non-current investment is an investment other than a 
current investment. 


०) Investments are initially recorded at cost and the cost includes acquisition costs such as 
brokerage, fees and duties. Accrued interest paid at the time of purchase is setoff against 
receipt of interest. 


d) Investments in the form of domestic government securities issued by Central and State 
Governments are available for use freely at the discretion of the Council except to the 
extent of total of the earmarked funds. 


e) At each balance sheet date, current investments are carried at lower of cost and fair 
value. The fair value is determined on an individual basis. The non-current investments 
are usually carried at cost. However, when there is a decline, other than temporary, in 
the value of a long term investment, the carrying amount is reduced to recognise the 
decline. The premium paid at the time of purchase is amortised over the remaining 
maturity of the investments. Amortisation of premium is adjusted against the 
income under head ‘Interest from Investments. 


Foreign Currency Transaction 


Transactions in foreign currencies are accounted at the exchange rates prevailing on the date 
of the transaction. 


Foreign currency monetary items outstanding at the balance sheet date are restated at the 
year-end rates. Non-monetary items are carried at historical cost. 


The Institute's foreign branch is considered an integral foreign operation. The financial 
statements of the branch are translated as if the transactions of the branch were those of the 
Institute. Monetary assets and liabilities are translated at the closing exchange rate, while non- 
monetary items are translated at historical exchange rates. Income and expenditure are 
translated at the exchange rates prevailing on the dates of the transactions or at average rates 
where such rates approximate the actual rates. Exchange differences arising on translation are 
recognised in the Statement of Income & Expenditure. 


Employee benefits 

Employee benefits include provident fund, gratuity, compensated absence, long service 
awards, pension scheme and post-employment medical benefits to eligible employees of the 
Institute. 


i) Short term employee benefits and other benefits 
The undiscounted amount of short-term employee benefits (i.e. salary, allowances, 
exgratia etc) expected to be paid in exchange for the services rendered by employees are 


322 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : EXTRAORDINARY [PART III—SEc.4] 


recognised during the year when the employees render the service. The short-term 
employee benefits are expected to occur within twelve months after the end of the period 
in which the eligible employee renders the related service. 


The cost of short-term compensated absences is accounted as under : 


a) Incase of accumulated compensated absences, when employees render the service 
that increase their entitlement of future compensated absences; and 


b) Incase of non-accumulating compensated absences, when the absences occur. 


ii) | Post-employment benefits 

Post-employment benefits are the benefits to eligible employees, other than termination 
benefits, which are payable after the completion of employment. Accounting of 
post-employment benefits depends upon the classification of relevant plans as either 
defined benefit plan (DBP) or defined contribution plan (DCP). The post-employment 
benefit plans where the Institute pays fixed contributions into a separate entity or fund 
and it will have no obligation to pay further contributions if the separate entity or fund 
does not hold sufficient assets to all employee benefits relating to employee service in 
the current and prior period. On the other hand, post-employment benefit plans other 
than those classified as DCP are classified as DBP. 


Defined Benefits Plans 


a) Gratuity 

For defined benefit plans in the form of gratuity, the cost of providing benefits is 
determined using the Projected Unit Credit Method, with actuarial valuations being carried 
out at each balance sheet date by an Independent Actuary. Actuarial gains and losses are 
recognised in the Statement of Income and Expenditure in the period in which they occur. 
Past service cost is recognised immediately to the extent that the benefits are already 
vested and otherwise is amortised on a straight-line basis over the average period until 
the benefits become vested. The retirement benefit obligation recognised represent the 
present value of the defined benefit obligation as adjusted for unrecognised past service 
cost, as reduced by the fair value of scheme assets. Any asset resulting from this 
calculation is limited to past service cost, plus the present value of available refunds and 
reductions in future contributions to the schemes. Gratuity liability is funded with Life 
Insurance Corporation of India. 


b) Provident Fund 

The contribution towards provident fund scheme to The Institute of Chartered 
Accountants of India Provident Fund Trust (‘the Trust’) is considered as defined benefit 
plan and charged as an expense based on the amount of contribution required to be 
made and when services are rendered by the eligible employees. The Trust is 
managed by the governing body elected by the Institute and settles claim of the 
employees as and when they arise. Any shortfall arising out of the actuarial liability of the 
PF Trust during the year is provided in the books of accounts. 


c) Pension scheme 
The Institute offers its eligible employees benefits in the form of pension and family 
pension. The present value of the obligation as at the balance sheet date is recognised 
based on the actuarial valuation. Pension liability is funded with Life Insurance Corporation 
of India.

d) Post retirement medical scheme benefit to retired employees and spouse 
The Institute offers employee benefits to its retired employees in the form of medical 
scheme.The present value of the obligation as at the balance sheet date is recognised 
based on the actuarial valuation of retired employees and their spouse as at reporting 
date. The liability is funded from the Employee Benevolent Fund. 


e) Other Long-term employee benefits- Compensated Absences 
Compensated absences which are not expected to occur within twelve months after the 
end of the period in which the employee renders the related service are recognised as a 
liability at the present value of the defined benefit obligation as at the balance sheet date 
based on the actuarial valuation. 


f) Long Service Award 
The Institute provides cash award to eligible employees on completion of specified years 
of serve and treated as long term employee benefits. The related liability is recognised 
based on actuarial valuation as at the balance sheet date and charged to statement of 
Income and Expenditure.

a) National Pension Scheme (NPS) 

The Institute contributes to the National Pension System (NPS), a defined contribution 
retirement benefit scheme administered by the Pension Fund Regulatory and 
Development Authority (PFRDA). Contributions made by the Institute are charged to the 
Statement of Income & Expenditure in the period in which the employee renders the 
related service. The Institute has no further obligation beyond making the specified 
contributions to the scheme. Unpaid contributions, if any, are recognized as a liability at 
the reporting date. 


Leases 

The Institute classifies the leases as Finance and Operating Lease for accounting and disclosure 
purposes. The leases where the Institute assumes substantially all the risks and rewards of the 
ownership are classified as finance leases. The leases where the lessor and not the Institute 
assumes substantially all the risks and rewards of the ownership are classified as operating 
leases. 


Lease rental under operating leases are recognised in the statement of income and expenditure 
on straight-line basis over the lease term. In case of Finance Lease, assets are capitalised at 
lower of fair value of the leased asset and present value of minimum lease payments. The lease 
payments are apportioned between the finance charge and repayment of lease liability. Leased 
assets are depreciated over the shorter of lease term or useful life of the asset. 


Impairment of Property, Plant and Equipment and intangible assets 

The carrying value of assets at each balance sheet date are reviewed for impairment. If any 
indication of impairment exists, the recoverable amount of such assets is estimated and 
impairment recognised, if the carrying amount of these assets exceeds their recoverable 
amount. The recoverable amount is the greater of the net selling price and their value in use. 
Value in use is arrived at by discounting the future cash flows to their present value based on 
an appropriate discount factor. When there is indication that an impairment loss recognised 
for an asset in earlier accounting periods no longer exists or may have decreased, such reversal 
of impairment loss is recognised in the statement of income and expenditure.

The Institute is registered under Clause (i) of First Proviso to Section 0(23C)/i2AB (i)(b) of 
The Income-tax Act, 96i valid up to financial year/tax year 2030-3.As such, no provision for 
current income tax and deferred tax is considered necessary. 


2.9 Provisions and Contingencies 
A provision is recognised when there is a present obligation as a result of past events and it is 
probable that an outflow of resources will be required to settle the obligation in respect of which 
a reliable estimate can be made. 


Contingent liability is a possible obligation that arises from past events and the existence of 
which will be confirmed only by the occurrence or non-occurrence of one or more uncertain 
future events not wholly within the control of the Institute, or is a present obligation that arises 
from past event but is not recognised because either it is not probable that an outflow of 
resources embodying economic benefits will be required to settle the obligation, or a reliable 
estimate of the amount of the obligation cannot be made. Based on the past experience of the 
Institute, when the possibility of outflow in settIment is remote, the contingent liability is not 
recognised . 


Contingent assets are neither recognised nor disclosed.

G.S.R. 698(E).— In exercise of the powers conferred by clauses (jaa) and (jab) of sub-section (2) of the section 
56, read with sub-section (.) and (2) of the section 3!AA of the Delhi Development Act, 957 (6] of 957), the Central 
Government and in consultation with the Authority hereby makes the following rules, namely: — 


l. Short title and commencement. —(l) These rules may be called the Delhi Development Authority (Manner of 
Holding Inquiry and Imposing Penalties) Rules 2026. 


(2) They shall come into force on the date of their publication in the Official Gazette. 
2. Definitions. — () In these rules, unless the context otherwise requires, — 
(a) "Act" means the Delhi Development Act, !957 (6! of 957); 
(b) "adjudicating officer" means an officer appointed under sub-section (l) of section 3lAA of the Act; 
(c) "appellate authority" means an officer appointed under sub- section (2) of section 3lAA of the Act; 
(d) "Form" means Form annexed to these rules. 


(2) The words and expressions used in these rules and not defined, but defined in the Act, shall have the meanings 
respectively assigned to them in the Act. 


3. Complainant. — Any person may file a complaint in Form | through electronic means or speed post to the 
adjudicating officer for imposing penalties regarding contravention committed under section 29 and sub-section (5) of 
section 3! of the Act. 


4. Holding of inquiry. — () For the purpose of adjudication of penalties under sub-section () of section 3lAA of the 
Act, on receipt of any complaint indicating any contravention of any provision of any section specified therein, the 
adjudicating officer shall, issue a notice in Form 2 to such person, requiring him to show cause within such period as 
may be specified in the notice (being not less than seven days from the date of service thereof) why an inquiry should 
not be held against him. 


(2) Every notice under sub-rule (() shall indicate the nature of contravention alleged to have been committed. 


(3) After considering the cause, if any, shown by such person, the adjudicating officer is of the opinion that an 
inquiry should be held, he shall issue a notice requiring the appearance of that person personally or through 
a representative duly authorised by him on such date as may be fixed in the notice. 


(4) On the date fixed, the adjudicating officer shall explain to the person proceeded against or his authorised 
representative, the contravention committed by such person and the provision of the Act, in respect of which 
contravention is alleged to have been committed. 


(5) The adjudicating officer shall, then, give an opportunity to such person to produce such documents or 
evidence under Form 3 as he may consider relevant to the inquiry, and if necessary, the hearing may be 
adjourned to a future date (not later than fifteen days from the first date and up to a maximum of three dates) 
and in taking such evidence the adjudicating officer shall not be bound to observe the provisions of the 
Bhartiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (47 of 2023). 


(6) If any person fails, neglects or refuses to appear as required under sub-rule (3) before the adjudicating 
officer, the adjudicating officer may proceed with the inquiry in the absence of such person after recording 
the reasons for doing so. 


(7) _ If, upon consideration of the evidence produced before the adjudicating officer, the adjudicating officer is 
satisfied that the person has committed the contravention, he may by order in writing, impose such penalty 
under the Act as applicable. 


(8) Every order made under sub-rule (7) shall specify the provision of the Act in respect of which contravention 
has been committed and shall contain the reasons for imposing the penalty. 


(9) Every order made under sub-rule (7) shall be dated and signed by the adjudicating officer. 


(0) A copy of the order made under this rule and all other copies of proceedings shall be supplied free of cost 
to the person against whom the inquiry was held.

The adjudicating officer shall complete the proceeding within three months from the issuance of the notice 
to the person against whom the inquiry was held. 


A notice or an order issued under these rules shall be served on the person against whom an inquiry is held, 
in any of the following manner, namely: — 


by delivering or tendering it to that person or his authorised representative; or 


by sending it to the person through electronic means or by speed post to the address of his place of residence 
or his last known place of residence or the place where he carried on or last carried on, business or personally 
works or last worked for gain; or 


If it cannot be served in the manner specified under clauses (i) or (ii), by affixing it on the outer door or 
some other conspicuous part of the premises in which that person resides or is known to have last resided 
or carried on business or personally works or has worked for gain. 


5. Appeal. — (l) An appeal under sub-section (2) of the section 3lAA of the Act shall be made to the appellate authority 
in Form 4 within a period of thirty days from the date of receipt of the order.

The appeal shall be accompanied by a copy of order of adjudicating officer and a statement of facts appealed 
against, the grounds for appeal and the relevant section of the Act. 


The appeal may be filed by the appellant in person or by his representative duly authorised in writing, or by 
speed post or through electronic means. 


The appeal sent by post shall be deemed to have been filed to the appellate authority on the day it is received. 


If on scrutiny, the appeal is found to be in order, it shall be admitted and in case the appeal is found to be 
defective, the appellate authority shall intimate the appellant about the defects and allow him to rectify the 
defects within fifteen days and if the appellant fails to rectify such defects within the time period, the 
appellate authority may by order and for reasons to be recorded in writing, decline to register such appeal 
and communicate such refusal to the appellant with a period of seven days thereof. 


On admission of the appeal, the appellate authority shall serve a copy of appeal to respondent along with a 
notice requiring him to file his reply thereto, within a period, not exceeding thirty days, as may be specified 
by the appellate authority in the said notice. 


The notice may be served by hand or by speed post or through electronic means. 
The appellate authority may call for the records relating to the proceedings from the adjudicating officer. 


The appellate authority may, after giving the parties to the appeal an opportunity of being heard, pass such 
orders as it may consider reasonable. 


The appellate authority shall dispose of the appeal within sixty days from the date of appeal. 


6. Extension of time.— The adjudicating officer or the appellate authority may, for reasons to be recorded in writing, 
where there is a reasonable cause for the delay or failure to act, extend any period specified in these rules till such period 
as it considers reasonable. 


7. Order and penalties. — () Every order under these rules, shall be dated, signed and communicated to all the parties 
and shall be placed in public domain through digital mode.

All sums realised by way of penalties under these rules shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India. 


If penalties imposed is not deposited within sixty days, then the adjudicating officer or appellate authority, 
as the case may be, may issue a certificate in Form 5, to the Collector who shall proceed to recover the same 
as an arrear of land revenue.

Scheme for Non-competitive Bidding Facility in the Auction of 
Government of India Dated Securities and Treasury Bills 
I. Scope: With a view to encouraging wider participation and retail holding of Government securities, retail 


investors are allowed participation on “non-competitive” basis in select auctions of dated Government of 
India (Gol) securities and Treasury Bills. 


IL. Definitions: For the purpose of this scheme, the terms shall bear the meaning assigned to them as under: 


a. Retail investor is any person, including individuals, firms, companies, corporate bodies, institutions, 
provident funds, trusts, and any other entity as may be prescribed by RBI. 
b. ‘Aggregator/Facilitator’ means a Scheduled Bank or Primary Dealer or Specified Stock Exchange or 
any other entity approved by RBI, permitted to aggregate the bids received from the investors and 
submit a single bid in the non-competitive segment of the primary auction. 
c. ‘Specified stock exchange’ means SEBI recognized Stock Exchange, which have received No 
Objection Certificate (NOC) from SEBI to act as aggregator/facilitator in the primary auction 


segment. 


d. ‘Eligible Provident Funds’ are those non-government provident funds governed by the Provident 


Funds Act, 925 whose investment pattern is decided by the Government of India. 


गा. Eligibility: 


a. Participation on a non-competitive basis in the auctions will be open to a retail investor who: 


l. Does not maintain current account (CA) or subsidiary General Ledger (SGL) account with the 
Reserve Bank of India; and 


2. Submits the bid indirectly through an Aggregator/Facilitator permitted under the scheme; or 
3. Maintains the ‘Retail Direct Gilt Account’ (RDG Account) with RBI 


Exceptions: 


a. Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) and Cooperative Banks: 


i. Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) and Cooperative Banks shall be covered under this Scheme only 
in the auctions of dated securities in view of their statutory obligations. 
li. Since these banks maintain SGL account and current account with the Reserve Bank of India, 
they shall be eligible to submit their non-competitive bids directly. 
b. State Governments, eligible provident funds and Others: 


i. State Governments, eligible provident funds in India, the Nepal Rashtra Bank, Royal Monetary 
Authority of Bhutan and any Person or Institution, specified by the Bank, with the approval of 
Government, shall be covered under this scheme only in the auctions of Treasury Bills. 


ii. These bids will be outside the notified amount. 


iii. There will not be any restriction on the maximum amount of bid for these entities.

five percent of the aggregate nominal amount of the issue within the notified amount as specified by the 


Government of India, or any other percentage determined by Reserve Bank of India. 


V. Amount of Bid: 


a. 


b.

In the auctions of Gol dated securities, the retail investors can make a single bid for an amount not 
more than Rupees Two crore (face value) per security per auction. 


VI. Other Operational Guidelines: 


a. 


The retail investor desirous of participating in the auction under the Scheme would be required to 
maintain a depository account with any of the depositories or a gilt account under the constituent 
subsidiary general ledger (CSGL) account of Aggregator/Facilitator or ‘Retail Direct Gilt Account’ 
(RDG Account) with RBI. 


Under the Scheme, an investor can make only a single bid in an auction. An undertaking to the 
effect that the investor is making only a single bid will have to obtained and kept on record by the 
Aggregator/Facilitator. 


Submission of Bids: 


Each Aggregator/Facilitator on the basis of firm orders received from their constituents with submit 
a single consolidated non-competitive bid on behalf of all its constituents in electronic format on the 
Reserve Bank of India Core Banking Solution (E-Kuber) system. Except in extraordinary 
circumstances such as general failure of the Reserve Bank of India Core Banking Solution (E- 
Kuber) system, non-competitive bid in physical form will not be accepted. 


Allotment of Bids: 


d. 


Allotment under the non-competitive segment to the Aggregator/Facilitator will be at the weighted 
average rate of yield/price that will emerge in the auction on the basis of the competitive bidding. 
The securities will be issued to the Aggregator/Facilitator against payment on the date of issue 
irrespective of whether they have received payment from their clients. 

In case the aggregate amount of bid is more than the reserved amount (5% of notified amount), pro 
rata allotment would be made. In case of partial allotments, it will be the responsibility of the 
Aggregator/Facilitator to appropriately allocate securities to their clients in a transparent manner. 

In case the aggregate amount of bids is less than the reserved amount, the shortfall will be taken to 
competitive portion. 


Issue of Security: 


g. 


Security would be issued only in SGL form by RBI. The Aggregator/Facilitator has to clearly 
indicate at the time of tendering the non-competitive bids the amounts (face value) to be credited to 
their main SGL or CSGL account. 

Delivery in physical form from the Main SGL account is permissible at the instance of the investor 
subsequently. 

It will be the responsibility of the Aggregator/Facilitator to pass on the securities to their clients. 
Except in extraordinary circumstances, the transfer of securities to the client should b completed 
within five working days from the date of issue.

New Delhi, the 3st July, 2026. 
Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Adjudication of Penalties Rules, 2026 


G.S.R. 699(E).—Whereas draft of the Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Adjudication of Penalties 
Rules, 2026, were published as required under sub-sections (l) and (2) of section 3] of the Coal Mines 
(Special Provisions) Act, 205 ([] of 205) in the Gazette of India, Extraordinary, Part II, Section 3, Sub- 
section (i) dated the 87 June, 2026 vide number G.S.R. 450(E), dated the 57 June, 2026 for information of 
all persons likely to be affected thereby; and notice was given that the said draft rules would be taken into 
consideration by the Central Government after the expiry of a period of fifteen days from the date on which 
copies of the Gazette containing the said rules were made available to the public; 


And whereas, suggestions or objections received in response to the above mentioned draft rules were 
considered by the Central Government; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (l) and clause (xa) of sub-section (2) 
of section 3l of the Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 20I5 ([] of 205), the Central Government 
hereby makes the following rules, namely: — 


l. Short title and commencement.— (l) These rules may be called the Coal Mines (Special 


Provisions) Adjudication of Penalties Rules, 2026. 
(2) They shall come into force on the date of their publication in the Official Gazette. 


2. Definitions.—(|) In these rules, unless the context otherwise requires,— 

(a) “Act” means the Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 20I5 (I of 20I5); 

(b) “adjudication authority” means the nominated authority appointed by the Central 
Government under sub-section (l) of section 24A of the Act; 

(c) “electronic means” includes email, a designated web-portal or any other digital platform 
specified by the Central Government; 

(d) “Form” means a Form appended to these rules; 

(e) “inquiry officer” means an officer, as designated under rule 4; 


THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : EXTRAORDINARY [PART I—SEC. 3(i)] 


(f) “inquiry proceeding” means proceedings initiated under section 24A of the Act. 
(2) Words and expressions used herein and not defined in these rules, but defined in the Act, 
shall have the meanings, respectively assigned to them in the Act. 


3. Holding of inquiry.— (() Where the adjudication authority has reason to believe that any 
person has committed a contravention of the Act liable for adjudication under section 24A of the 
Act, it may, either suo motu or upon receipt of a complaint or report, initiate inquiry proceedings. 
(2) For the purpose of conducting an inquiry under sub-rule (), the adjudication authority may— 

(a) call for information, records, books, registers, returns or documents from any person; 

(b) require the attendance of any person acquainted with the facts and circumstances of the 
case; 

(c) seek written explanations or statements; 

(d) obtain inspection reports or technical reports from any Government agency, expert 
body, technical institution, and the likes. 

(3) The adjudication authority shall record reasons for initiation of proceedings conducted under 
sub-rule (). 

4. Inquiry Officer and secretariat assistance to the adjudication authority— (.) For the 
purpose of inquiry proceedings, the adjudication authority shall designate an officer not below the 
rank of an Under Secretary to the Government of India having knowledge of the facts and 
circumstances constituting the contravention as the Inquiry Officer to assist the adjudication 
authority. 

(2) The Central Government shall designate such officers, staff, consultants or agencies, as may be 
necessary to provide secretarial, technical or administrative assistance to the adjudication authority 
for the discharge of its functions under the Act and these rules. 


5. Issue of notice.— (]) Where the adjudication authority is satisfied that there exists a prima facie 
case for inquiry, it shall issue a notice in Form-I to the person alleged to have committed the 
contravention. 

(2) The notice shall contain— 
(a) the nature of the contravention alleged; 
(b) the relevant provisions of the Act or rules alleged to have been violated; 
(c) the material relied upon; 
(d) the time within which a written reply is to be furnished. 
(3) The notice shall ordinarily provide a period of not less than fifteen days and not more than 
thirty days for submission of a reply. 


6. Service of notice and orders. — (l) Any notice, communication or order under these rules may 
be served by— 
(a) speed post with registration and proof of delivery; 
(b) electronic means; 
(c) delivery by hand against receipt; or 
(d) any other mode as the adjudication authority may deem fit. 
(2) Service by electronic means shall be deemed valid where transmitted to the email address 
or digital account furnished by the concerned person to the Central Government, nominated 
authority or any other statutory authority. 


7. Filing of reply and appearance. — (l) The noticee may file a written reply along with 
supporting documents within the time specified in the notice. 
(2) The noticee may appear in person or through an authorised representative.

(3) The adjudication authority may permit to file the additional documents or written 
submissions upon sufficient cause being shown. 


Hearing. — (l) The adjudication authority shall provide the noticee a reasonable opportunity of 
being heard. 
(2) The hearing may be conducted physically or through electronic means. 
(3) If the noticee fails to appear despite due service of notice, the adjudication authority may 
proceed ex parte after recording reasons thereof. 
(4) Where, during the course of hearing, the adjudication authority considers that further 
inquiry is required, it may adjourn the proceedings and call for additional material. 


Factors for the determination of penalty. — While adjudging the quantum of penalty under 
section 24A, the adjudication authority shall have due regard to the following factors, namely: — 

(a) the nature, gravity and duration of the contravention; 

(b) the repetitive nature of default; 

(c) the amount of gain or unfair advantage derived from the contravention, wherever 

quantifiable; 

(d) the loss or damage caused to public interest or Government’s revenue; 

(e) whether the contravention was wilful, fraudulent or mala fide; 

(f) the conduct of the person during the inquiry, including the cooperation extended; 

(g) any steps taken for mitigation or rectification of the default. 


Order by adjudication authority. — (|) After considering the reply, evidence on record and 
submissions made during the hearing, the adjudication authority shall pass a reasoned order. 
(2) The order shall contatin— 
(a) brief facts; 
(b) issues for determination; 
(c) findings with reasons; 
(d) the penalty imposed, if any; and 
(e) the time within which the penalty shall be paid. 
(3) A copy of the order shall be served upon the concerned person in accordance with rule 6. 


Payment and recovery of penalty. — (l) The penalty imposed under these rules shall be paid 

within thirty days from the date of receipt of the order or within such extended period, as may be 

allowed by the adjudication authority for reasons to be recorded in writing. 

(2) The amount of penalty shall be deposited through such mode and under such head of account, 
as may be specified by the Central Government. 

(3) In case of failure to pay the penalty within the stipulated period, the amount shall be 
recoverable in accordance with sub-section (4) of section 24B of the Act. 


Residual powers. — Save as provided, the adjudication authority may regulate its own 
procedure in a manner consistent with the principles of natural justice and in accordance with the 
provisions of the Act.
